newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac visits Cannes as centre-right gains in poll.
newsitem.headline: Chirac visits Cannes as centre-right gains in poll.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac visited the Cannes film festival on Sunday during a parliamentary election campaign which could make or break the last five years of his term.

He assumed a sharply higher public profile as a new poll published on Sunday showed his centre-right government building on its lead over the left two weeks before the first-round vote in the May 25-June 1 snap parliamentary election.
Political analyst Jean-Luc Parodi of the IFOP polling institute noted, however, that 27 percent of the registered voters surveyed said they may yet change their minds.
Further, each percentage-point shift in voter preference could swing as many as 30 seats in the National Assembly, Parodi cautioned.
Chirac was the first French president to visit the glitzy annual film festival in southern France, which this year has been celebrating its 50th anniversary.
He lunched at the Palais des Festivals with the Cannes jury and a bevy of past award winners, seated between stars Isabelle Adjani of France and Gong Li of China.
In an earlier high-profile move, a beaming Chirac went to Paris' Parc des Princes stadium on Saturday evening to watch the French soccer cup final.
Millions of voters looked on via live television as Chirac shook hands with both teams and then joined the exuberant crowd.

The IFOP poll for the weekly Journal du Dimanche, conducted on Friday, gave the centre-right 41 percent of the vote, up three points from a similar poll a week earlier, to 38.5 for the combined left, a 2.5-point dip from the previous week.
It projected the centre-right would win at least a 100-seat National Assembly majority due in part to the magnifying effect of the two-round voting system in single-member constituencies.

Earlier polls had shown the left gaining steadily on the centre-right, stirring unease in Chirac's camp and triggering a round of sniping by coalition allies against Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who has been leading the government campaign.

Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, touring a Paris marketplace in search of votes on Sunday, said the polls' ups and downs showed the French people were still examining the various parties' competing claims.
"The French people are unhappy with the current situation. The current government is extremely unpopular...but at the same time it seems they are a bit afraid of change," Jospin said.

"The worst, after four years of the current majority, would be to keep them for another five years," Jospin said. "So I urge you to think about it, make up your minds, but if the French people hope to regain their sense of the future, they must dare to change."

European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier charged in a televised debate that the Socialists were willing to risk derailing the shift to a single European currency to protect a shaky alliance with France's Communists, who oppose European monetary union.

"I find that you are in danger of compromising the single currency, and even more serious, compromising our friendship with Germany, in order to protect your campaign alliance," Barnier said during a campaign debate with Socialist Elisabeth Guigou on France 2 television.
But Guigou said the Socialists wanted only to assure, before adopting the euro currency, that it served the interests of Europeans and would not worsen France's record 12.8 percent unemployment.
